Body: _The following comment was made by an LLM, it may be inaccurate:_

Corroborating this at scale — same mechanism, 44 instances, with a controlled reproduction.

**Loss signature.** Scanning the local session store for "child terminal >60 s after its last delivered `<subagent>` notification" finds 44 instances: 2 on 2026-09-10 (beta-19425), 1 on 09-23, 23 on 09-24, 18 on 09-25. Every loss sits on a child that had been resumed or re-woken; fresh-spawn first completions were delivered correctly every time, matching the report.

**One fully-traced instance.** Parent resumed a background child at 17:08; the drain's first idle fired the notification at 17:42:58. A second call from the parent at 17:41:10 (admitted while the child was busy) promoted as a successor turn after that idle. Final idle: 17:45:25 — no notification, ever. Parent had gone idle at 17:44:56; its inbox was empty and pending count 0 (never posted, not queued).

**Controls.** No service restart in the window (single run id across the log). Error drains still notify — a child whose drain failed on 2026-09-25 delivered two notifications. Empty inbox rules out queue-promotion loss.

**Controlled reproduction.** Spawned a test orchestrator-type agent as a subagent with one background child. Its first idle landed 2 s before the child's completion notification; the parent received the interim text as final. The child's real verdict turn (26 s later) was invisible by construction, recovered only via `GET /api/session/{id}/message` readback.

**Mechanism (hypothesis consistent with all observations):** the background job's watcher fires at the child's *first idle after the parent's call* and is consumed. Any later drain — steer/queue-promoted successor, or a wake from a `<shell state="completed">` synthetic — is owned by no job, so its terminal event injects nothing. The delivered notification is additionally *prematurely terminal*: the parent is told `completed` at an intermediate idle while the real final state lands later, unseen.

**Exposure note.** Local loss rate went ~2 per 2 weeks → 41 in 2 days when the fleet moved all lead→worker dispatch to background on 09-24. Can share a sanitized per-instance table — timestamps, opaque session IDs, and outcome fields only; no paths, project names, or transcripts — plus the SQL signature behind the scan, if useful for triage.

Corroborating with a fully-traced instance of the exact shape described.

Worker with pending background shell processes: parent notified `state="completed"` at 14:57. The background shell finished at 15:22:07 — the child's transcript shows the wake source explicitly: a `<shell id=… state="completed">` synthetic at 15:22:07, followed by a final verification turn and the real final report, idle at 15:26:23. Never delivered; the answer was stranded exactly as described. The parent then held its turn ~2.5 h (~200 no-op turns) waiting for a result that had already happened.

**Recovery today is only out-of-band:** `GET /api/session/{id}/message` readback. Parent agents cannot self-detect this — the only ground truth is the HTTP API, and agent-side `webfetch`/Code-Mode `fetch` cannot authenticate to it (401 without CLI credentials), so there is no agent-facing way to ask "what is my child's actual state?"

**Population.** Same local scan as the sibling reports: 44 instances of "terminal >60 s after last notification" over 09-10 → 09-25 (v2.0.16 back to beta-19425); losses concentrate on children with background shells or resumes; fresh-spawn first completions always delivered. Error-drain controls still notify, so it is not the drain-failure path.

Can share the same sanitized form for this instance — event types, timestamps, opaque IDs, and the synthetic injection points only; no transcripts, paths, or project names.

---
This issue might be a duplicate of existing issues. Please check:
- #51274: Reports the same `request_preview` failure with “Relay tunnel is not connected” when creating a public preview URL.
previsão para a conexão?

---
This issue might be a duplicate of existing issues. Please check:
- #36778: multiple authenticated accounts per provider with automatic rate-limit and quota failover.
- #8591: automatic credential rotation within the same provider, including support for plugin authors.
- #11830: multi-account OAuth support with automatic failover.

That constant ~2050 token count is a great catch and strong sign the tool schemas just aren't making it into the subagent's request at all. I've been working on a CLI (Polyglot, my own project) built around this exact failure - local models narrating a plausible result instead of actually calling a tool. gpt-oss saying "I can't run commands" and then fabricating a commit hash is a perfect example of it.

I'm curious about what you're building - would you be up for a quick 15-min chat?

I ran the focused model-catalog test on this head:

`cd packages/core && bun test test/models.test.ts`
→ 12 pass / 0 fail

The behavior matches the intended boundary in the tested scope: a models.dev fetch failure can fall back to an empty catalog without killing bootstrap, while later refresh remains able to repopulate it.

I didn't independently exercise a full cold-start Desktop session here, so this is focused behavioral evidence rather than an end-to-end startup claim.

I ran the focused process suite on this head:

`cd packages/core && bun test test/process/process.test.ts`
→ 27 pass / 0 fail

The tested invariant looks right: completion follows the direct child process exit rather than waiting indefinitely for descendant-held stdio, including the covered output/stream paths.

I haven't independently reproduced the full real descendant-process hang outside the test harness, so treating this as focused behavioral evidence rather than full E2E proof.

```
#0  opencode + 0x2407064       ; ud2
#5  libopentui.so + 0x1d061d   ; OptimizedBuffer.trySetTransparentTextCellFast, buffer.zig:896
```

I took a closer look at the cross-process refresh regression on head 00aee1daed.

The useful part is that this is testing more than a normal OAuth refresh:

- it constructs two separate providers sharing the same EffectFlock state directory
- it uses plain fetch, so the providers do not share an in-memory single-flight request
- the token endpoint deliberately holds the first refresh open
- the observed refresh-token sequence must be r, then r+
- the final stored refresh token must be r++

That pins the important ownership invariant: the waiter has to re-read the credential after acquiring the lock rather than replaying the refresh token that the previous holder just rotated.

The exact-head check and test workflows are green.

The remaining limit I see is that the regression uses separate provider instances sharing the filesystem lock rather than two real OS processes against an IdP with reuse detection. That feels like qualification evidence rather than a missing unit-level contract, assuming EffectFlock cross-process exclusion is already covered at its owner.

I checked the failure-accounting cases on head c0fd5c452c more closely.

The regressions pin three different outcomes:

- five idle-timeout failures cause the sixth request to stay on HTTP, with only five WebSocket opens

That distinction looks important. The breaker is counting actual failed exchanges, not simply every non-terminal stream exit, and interruption does not poison the transport.

I compared this directly with #46023 because the duplicate bot flags them as the same fix.

They overlap on locking + atomic auth.json writes, but there is one important difference: #46023 still has its mutation path read through the OPENCODE_AUTH_CONTENT override.

That means a workspace child holding a stale auth snapshot can still mutate one credential and persist that stale snapshot back to disk, dropping credentials added after the child was spawned.

This branch separates those semantics:

- Auth.all/get may still honor OPENCODE_AUTH_CONTENT for inherited reads.
- Auth.set/remove read the actual file while holding the auth lock.
- the mutation is then atomically renamed into place.

The regression for "set reads the file instead of persisting the auth env snapshot" specifically pins that second failure mode, which #46023 does not appear to cover.

So I would not treat these as exact duplicates. #46023 covers concurrent/atomic persistence; this PR additionally fixes stale inherited-auth state becoming write authority.
